Neonatal North American river otters (Lontra canadensis) are remarkably well-developed, entering the world with their eyes open and a full coat of fur. The average pup weighs approximately 140 grams [Wwb = approximately 140 grams] at birth, a substantial mass that reflects their precocial developmental strategy. At the species' typical core body temperature of 38.4 °C [T = 38.4 °C], gestation is completed in roughly 62 days [tg = roughly 62 days], a duration that, while short, aligns with the rapid embryogenesis observed in many mustelids. This relatively abbreviated gestation is balanced by an extended period of postnatal dependence following parturition, during which the altricial neonate transitions to a milk-based diet through suckling onset. The substantial birth mass provides a crucial energy reserve, allowing the newborn to maintain stable thermoregulation in aquatic environments from its earliest days of life, a necessity for a species born in natal dens near water.

Females typically give birth to a single litter each year, producing an average of 2.9 pups per litter [N_R_i = 2.9 pups per litter] and maintaining a reproductive frequency of 0.9 litters per year [F_R_i = 0.9 litters per year], a combination that yields a relatively low annual reproductive output compared to smaller mustelids. The nursing pups remain wholly dependent on their mother's milk during the early stages of the suckling juvenile period, with nutritional independence beginning only after several months. Under the same thermal conditions maintained throughout their active life (38.4 °C [T = 38.4 °C]), the time since birth at weaning is exactly 122 days [tx = 122 days], marking the point at which offspring transition from a diet of milk to solid food, primarily fish and aquatic invertebrates. This extended period of maternal investment is typical of a species that must teach its young sophisticated hunting techniques in complex aquatic habitats.

Following the weaning process, the now nutritionally independent juveniles enter a prolonged growth phase as they develop the body mass and hunting proficiency needed for survival. During this juvenile stage, individuals exhibit a rapid increase in body weight, approaching adult dimensions over many months. By the time they reach about 730 days since birth [tp = about 730 days since birth], a landmark achieved at a core body temperature of 38.4 °C [T = 38.4 °C], most females attain sexual maturation, marking the onset of puberty and the beginning of their reproductive potential. Males follow a similar trajectory, also reaching puberty at approximately 730 days since birth [tp = approximately 730 days since birth], a delay that ensures they have achieved sufficient body size and competitive ability before attem at a temperature of 38.4 °C [T = 38.4 °C]pting to breed. This concordance in the timing of reproductive maturity between the sexes is somewhat unusual among mustelids.

Adult body size in Lontra canadensis displays considerable sexual dimorphism, with females reaching an ultimate wet weight of about 8.3 kilograms [Wwi = about 8.3 kilograms], while males are substantially larger, attaining an ultimate wet weight of approximately 11.3 kilograms [Wwi = approximately 11.3 kilograms]. Some exceptionally large males can reach masses up to 15 kilograms [Wwi = 15 kilograms], likely reflecting optimal foraging conditions in prey-rich territories. By the time weaning concludes, the average pup has grown to a wet weight at weaning of 1510 grams [Wwx = 1510 grams], representing a greater than tenfold increase over its birth mass and demonstrating the efficiency of maternal lactation. This rapid mass gain is crucial, as the young must achieve a substantial fraction of adult size before their first winter to survive the energetic demands of cold-water foraging.

The overall life history of the North American river otter is characterized by a slow pace for a mustelid of its size, with a maximum lifespan of 27 years [am = 27 years] when measured at a core body temperature of 38.4 °C [T = 38.4 °C]. This considerable longevity is linked to their position as top predators in aquatic ecosystems, where mortality risks from predators are low but energetic costs of thermoregulation are high. Interestingly, the maximum recorded reproductive rate consists of approximately 2.9 pups per litter [N_R_i = approximately 2.9 pups per litter] and 0.9 litters per year [F_R_i = 0.9 litters per year], a low annual fecundity that is compensatory with their long lifespan. This demographic strategy, favoring adult survival and iteroparity over high fecundity, is typical of large-bodied, long-lived carnivores and is reflected in their highly structured social systems and strong territorial behaviors.
